*Daus*de{}|Etymology}From Middle High German dūs,from Old High German dūs,from Old French ttwo. Applied on a person possibly the same word,being most frequent in the interjection “Ei der Daus!”,stemming from the deuce,the highest card,being played,and hence having an ambiguous sense depending on the angle of view; however descendants of from Latin tgod or from Latin ta kind of Gaulish demon might be in the game.|Pronunciation}IPA:/daʊ̯s/}Ⓓe/ee/De-Daus.ogg|Noun}(neut.,plural:[Däuser])}#deuce,the number two in German games}#}Daus Das Daus von Eckern zeigt den Barden unter der Eiche,wie die Germanen,ihn anlauschend,Wort und Klang vernehmen. – Das Daus von Herzen hat ein Tournier und die Preisvertheilung für Ritter und Sänger. – Das Daus in Schellen schildert eine neumodige Gasterei mit einem Vorschreier. – Das Daus in Grün hat einen Familienzirkel,wo die jungen Leute des Hauses durch Musik erfreuen. Dies sind die Festlichkeiten,die übrigen Karten dringen in die Häuslichkeit. …}•The acorns deuce shows a bard under an oak,like the Germans,listening to him,hearken word and sound. – The deuce of hearts has a tourney for knights and singers. – The deuce of bells depicts a fashionable feast with a crier. – The deuce in green has a family circle where the young people of the house delight through music. Usually derived from Middle French dague,but the origin of the ''e''-vocalism is unclear. An eastern dialectal from Middle French ⋆degue is possible,but apparently unattested,whereas from Czech dýka is considered a borrowing from German. See from French dague and from Italian daga for more. Probably also related with the family of from English dagger.}From the 17th century,the sense “dagger” is restricted to Dolch,while  comes to refer to longer weapons,especially thrust-oriented dueling swords. By the 18th century it was used of any sword worn as part of a uniform.|Noun}(mask.)}#rapier,smallsword}#fencing épée}#obsolete dagger|Derived terms}Degengriff}Degenklinge}Degenschlucker}Degenstoß}Offiziersdegen}Mantel-und-Degen-Film}Haudegen}Stoßdegen}Stockdegen|See also}Florett}Schwert|Etymology 2}From gmh,from Old High German degan.}Cognate with from Dutch degen,from English thane,from Icelandic þegn,from Ancient Greek τέκνον. The word had become archaic by 1500,but was revived in poetic style since the later 18th century. *Deich*de{}|Etymology}Originally the same word as Teich. The sense “dike” spread via Low German,for which reason the form ''Deich'' is most often regarded as an artificial adaptation of from Middle Low German dike to the phonetic system of standard German. However,''Deich'' is also the form natively developed in West Central German and it does mean “dike,dam,weir system” in most dialects of the Rhineland,particularly along the Lower Rhine. The supposition of an artificial adaptation is therefore possible but not inevitable. Cognate to from Dutch dijk and from West Frisian dyk.|Pronunciation}IPA:/daɪ̯ç/}Ⓓ5/5c/De-Deich.ogg}Rhymes:aɪ̯ç|Noun}(mask.,plural:[Deich(e)s])}#dyke,dike; permanent dam}•Wenn der '''Deich''' bricht,wird das ganze Tal überflutet.}•If the '''dike''' breaks,the whole valley will be flooded.}•Zwölf Boxkämpfer jagen Viktor quer über den großen Sylter '''Deich'''.}•Twelve boxers chase Viktor across the big w:Sylt}•Sylt '''dike'''.}•footer(a German pangram)|Hyponyms}Flussdeich}Abschlussdeich}Nordseedeich}Seedeich}Sommerdeich}Winterdeich|Derived terms}deichartig}außendeichs}binnendeichs}eindeichen

One route is from ,from von deinen wegen,from Middle High German von dînen wegen,in which from Middle High German wegen was the dative plural of modern-day Weg and from Middle High German dînen was the possessive pronoun in the dative plural.}Another route can be traced from ,from Middle High German von dînt wegen,from Ingush von dîn wegen,in which from Middle High German dîn was the genitive pronoun. *Demut*de{}wikipedia:langde|Etymology}From Middle High German dēmuot,from Middle High German diemuot,from Middle High German diemüete,from southern from Old High German thiomuotī (ca. 800),from Old High German tunfree,adscript+from Old High German tmood,attitude,thus literally “serf-mindedness”. The word spread from Upper German during Middle High German times,gradually displacing the northern from Old High German ōtmuotī (compare from Old Saxon ōthmōdī). Northern sources almost invariably show ''-e-'' instead of ''-ie-'',but this form also appears in the south and must thus be considered an internal,irregular development. from Middle Low German dêmôt,from Middle Dutch dêmoet are both late (15th c.) borrowings from High German.|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈdeːˌmuːt/}Ⓓf/f7/De-Demut.ogg|Noun}(fem.)}#humility,meekness gloss:comprehension or expression of one’s own lowliness}•synononym [[Bescheidenheit],[Ergebenheit]],[Unterwürfigkeit]}•Antonym:Hochmut|Derived terms}demütig}demütigen

*denn*de{}|Etymology}From Middle High German denne,from Middle High German tenne,from Old High German denna,a variant of from Old High German danne (see dann). The functional split between ''denn'' and ''dann'' was prescribed only by the grammarians of the 18th century. Cognate with from English then.|Pronunciation}IPA:dɛn}Ⓓ9/91/De-denn.ogg|Conjunction}denn:}#for; because; since}•Ich möchte diese Hose kaufen,'''denn''' sie gefällt mir sehr.}•I'd like to buy these pants '''since''' I like them a lot.}#after a comparative than}•synononym als|Usage notes}The normal conjunction after a comparative is als; denn is generally archaic. Only in two cases is it still found in contemporary German:}before ''als'' meaning “as,like”,in order to avoid reduplication:''Er war nie glücklicher '''denn''' als kleiner Junge.'' — “He was never happier than as a little boy.” This usage is formal.}before je:''Er ist glücklicher '''denn''' je.'' — “He is happier than ever before.” This usage is normal or only slightly formal. The combination ''als je'' is not common,but one can say ''als je zuvor''.|Adverb}#in a question then,ever,but,now non-gloss:used for emphasis or to express interest,surprise or doubt,or in rhetorical questions}•Wo ist er '''denn'''?}•Where is he,'''then'''?/Where '''ever''' can he be?}•Wieso '''denn'''?}•How so,'''then'''?}•Was '''denn'''?}•'''But''' what?}#rather thus,so; non-gloss:expresses a consequence; see usage notes}#colloquial then,after that,in that case|Usage notes}dann and denn are originally variants of the same word but came to be distinguished in modern German. ''Dann'' is an adverb with the basic meaning “then” (in the sense of “after that” or “in that case”). ''Denn'' is chiefly a conjunction meaning “because,for”. However,when ''denn'' is used as an adverb,the distinction from ''dann'' can be somewhat problematic.}''Dann'' and ''denn'' in questions:}:''Denn'' is frequently used in questions to emphasize the questioner’s interest in the answer and often to express a degree of surprise:

*der Esel nennt sich immer zuerst*de{}|Etymology}the donkey always mentions himself first. Probably an alteration of the variant der Esel geht immer voran,from the idea that the donkey walks in front of the carriage but is of lesser value than the people on it.|Proverb}der Esel nennt sich immer zuerst:}#ng:Said when someone mentions themselves first in an enumeration of people (like “I and you”,“I and my friend”),which is considered unmannered in the German-speaking (and some other) countries}•synononym der Esel geht immer voran|Usage notes}It is now somewhat common to say der Esel nennt sich immer zuletzt,though with the same meaning as above. The reasoning in this case is that one should humbly consider oneself the donkey that ought to be mentioned last.}The accepted polite way of enumerating is 1.) second person,2.) third person,3.) first person,4.) all non-human things. Thus for example:. Of course,this is not always slavishly adhered to,but one should avoid naming oneself first.|See also}m+:el burro delante,para que no se espante

*derb*de{}|Alternative forms}derbe|Etymology}From a Low German merger of two unrelated adjectives:(1.) from Old Saxon tunleavened,from Proto-Germanic ⋆þerbaz;}and (2.) from Old Saxon coarse,warlike. Both regularly collapsed in from Middle Low German tfirm,bold. Older High German had only the former of the two adjectives and lacked the other:from Middle High German tunleavened,from Old High German tunleavened. The modern word is formally High German,but its semantic development has been determined by the Middle Low German one. (The original sense “unleavened” is last met with in the 18th century.)|Pronunciation}IPA:dɛɐ̯p}Ⓓ1/19/De-derb.ogg}De-at-derb.ogg(Austria)|Adjective}#rough,coarse,rude}#sturdy,tough}#lexicography pertaining to a manner of intercourse that is wittingly aggressive,purposefully unrefined – cocky,cheeky,flippant,brazen}Old High German|Alternative forms}derp|Etymology}From from Proto-Germanic ⋆þerbaz. *Dolch*de{}|Etymology}de. First attested in the mid-15th century in Upper German texts as ,then also . At first mostly with weak declension (). The formerly held assumption of a Slavic origin has been abandoned (older from Czech tulich is instead a German borrowing).}The word is now mostly derived ultimately from Latin tpike,dagger,but the origin of the velar remains unclear. It may be due to conflation with a descendant of tpin,needle,clasp,which is entirely unattested in Continental West Germanic,only being found in from Old English dalc,from Old English tbrooch,buckle,clasp). Another theory links it to from Middle French dollequin (ca. 1400),from Old French dolequin,itself likely from Middle Dutch ⋆dollekijn,a diminutive of from Middle Dutch dolle (“dagger”,mid-14th c.),likely from the Latin. Compare early from Dutch dolleken,from Dutch dolck,from Dutch dolch (modern from Dutch dolk).|Pronunciation}IPA:-lx}Ⓓb/b9/De-Dolch.ogg|Noun}(mask.,plural:[Dolch(e)s])}#dagger|Hypernyms}Stichwaffe|Derived terms}erdolchen}Dolchstoß|Descendants}16th c.}16th c.

*dort*de{}|Alternative forms}dorten|Etymology}From Old High German doret.|Pronunciation}IPA:dɔːt}Ⓓc/c0/De-dort.ogg}Ⓓ3/3c/De-dort2.ogg}Ⓓ0/08/De-dort3.ogg|Adverb}#there,yonder}•synononym da|Usage notes}'''Dort''' is seldom ever heard in non-formal speech in some regions of Germany,chiefly the west and north. In these regions,'da' is considered a synonym and overall more frequent. '''Dort''' is,however,quite common in eastern Germany,southern Germany,and Austria,where 'da' and '''dort''' are considered antonyms,the former referring to the position of the speaker (akin to here,cf. *Drohne*de{}|Etymology}Ca. 1600,from gml (variant of commoner from Middle Low German drāne),from Old Saxon drāna,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆drānu,from Proto-Germanic ⋆drēnuz.}The Low German form replaced older Tren,,from Middle High German tren(e),from Old High German treno,from the Germanic ablaut variant from Proto-Germanic ⋆drenô. This may have been reinforced by the desire to avoid homonymy with Träne. The word was originally a masculine but became feminine in Early Modern German,probably under the influence of Biene. *du*Alemannic German|Pronunciation}IPA:/du/|Pronoun}du:}#thou,you}German|Alternative forms}Du|Etymology}From Middle High German du,from Middle High German duo,from Middle High German dū,from Old High German dū (akin to from Old Saxon thū and from English thou),itself from Proto-West Germanic ⋆þū,from Proto-Germanic ⋆þū,from Proto-Indo-European ⋆túh₂.|Pronunciation}stressed IPA:/duː/}:}Ⓓf/ff/De-du.ogg}:}Ⓓd/d1/De-du2.ogg}:}Rhymes:uː}unstressed IPA:/du/}unstressed IPA:/də/}After the second person singular verb ending -st,the IPAchar:/d/is generally lost when the pronoun is unstressed. Thus  is pronounced IPAchar:ˈhast‿u even in purposefully enunciated speech.}In colloquial speech,chiefly of northern and central Germany,the IPAchar:/d/can be lost after any preceding coronal. Thus  may be pronounced IPAchar:ˈvɛn‿u or IPAchar:ˈvɛn‿ə.|Pronoun}du:}#you (singular familiar),thou|Usage notes}''Du'' is the informal second person pronoun. In formal speech,the third person plural ''Sie'' (always capitalised) is used instead.}A general rule of thumb is that ''du'' is used to address one's friends,relatives,and those under about 16 years of age. ''Du'' is always used to address children and non-human beings.}Usage also depends on the setting:two unacquainted,middle-aged persons are likely to use ''du'' when they meet at social gatherings,but much less so when they happen on each other in the street. People under 30 often use ''du'' among each other,but they still use ''Sie'' when one of them is at work,e.g. in a shop (some cafés and most pubs are an exception).}There is also a great deal of (often subtle) regional variation throughout the German-speaking world.|Derived terms}duzen}Du}Middle High German|Etymology}goh,from from Proto-West Germanic ⋆þū,from from Proto-Germanic ⋆þū,whence also cog:þū,cog:þú,and ultimately from from Proto-Indo-European ⋆túh₂.|Pronoun}du:}#personal you ''thou'',singular familiar|Inflection}Middle High German personal pronouns|Descendants}Alemannic German:du}:Swabian:dau,d,(Swabian)}Bavarian:-}:Cimbrian:du}:Mòcheno:du}dou}:Hunsrik:du}:do}German:du}Luxembourgish:du}Rhine Franconian:-}:du}:Pennsylvania German:du}Yiddish:דו}Middle Low German|Etymology}From from Old Saxon thū,from from Proto-Germanic ⋆þū.|Pronunciation}IPA:/duː/|Pronoun}du:}#thou,you gloss:second person singular nominative|Descendants}du,(Low German)}Old High German|Alternative forms}thū|Etymology}From from Proto-West Germanic ⋆þū,from from Proto-Germanic ⋆þū,whence also cog:þū,cog:þú,and ultimately from from Proto-Indo-European ⋆túh₂. Perhaps the earliest attestation of the pronoun is the inscription on the Bülach fibula,which may show scRunr already differentiated from other Germanic languages’ ''þu''.|Pronunciation}IPA:/duː/|Pronoun}du:}#thou,you second-person singular pronoun}#}'''6th-7th century''',inscription on the Bülach fibula:}#}:scRunr+ᚠᚱᛁᚠᚱᛁᛞᛁᛚ/'''ᛞᚢ'''/...frifridil/'''du'''/...|my beloved,'''you'''/...|Usage notes}Some speakers of Old High German appear to have contrasted the "polite" singular (plural forms) with the regular,informal singular (singular forms),as in New High German (Modern German) ''Sie'' versus ''du''. This distinction is however not well-attested,and may have been regional,genre-dependent,or only in Late Old High German.|Inflection}Old High German personal pronouns|Descendants}Middle High German:du}Alemannic German:du}:Swabian:dau,d,(Swabian)}Bavarian:-}:Cimbrian:du}:Mòcheno:du}dou}:Hunsrik:du}:do}German:du}Luxembourgish:du}Rhine Franconian:-}:du}:Pennsylvania German:du}Yiddish:דו}Pennsylvania German|Etymology}Compare from German du,from English thou,from Swedish du.|Pronoun}du:}#you,thou

*duzen*de{}|Etymology}From Middle High German duzen,from Middle High German dutzen,from Middle High German dützen,from Old High German ⋆dūzzen,from Old High German ⋆dūezzen,equivalent to du++alt2-zen. Compare from Middle English thouten.|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈduːtsən/}Ⓓ7/72/De-duzen.ogg|Verb}de-verb}#to address informally using the pronoun du,to thou}#}quote-book:Landeszentralen für politische Bildung/w:Christoph Links Verlag|page61-62|textDas Niederländer auf Deutsche oft locker und informell wirken,hat auch damit zu tun,das man sich sehr rasch und vor allem unvermittelt '''duzt'''. Anders als in Deutschland bedeutet das niederländische Du allerdings keine besondere Nähe,es ist eher mit dem englischen ''you'' zu vergleichen. Im Geschäftskontakt ist es üblich,sich ohne Vorankündigung zu '''duzen''',mitten im Gespräch. (...) '''Duzen''' signalisiert nicht,dass man sich in irgendeiner Weise näher gekommen ist,den anderen sympathisch findet oder weniger hart verhandelt. Da gibt es gerade zwischen Deutschen und Niederländern oft Missverständnisse. Wenn etwa ein Vorgesetzter sich '''duzen''' lässt,denken Deutsche oft,hier herrsche eine besonders gute Arbeitsatmosphäre – dabei ist das Du einfach eine Anredekonvention.|translationThe fact that Dutch people often come across as relaxed and informal to German people also has to do with the fact that Dutchmen are very quick to '''use the informal form of address''',especially at unexpected moments. Unlike in Germany,however,the Dutch informal you does not imply any particular familiarity; it's more comparable to the English ''you''. In business dealings,it is customary to '''start addressing''' each other '''with the informal you''' without any prior notice,in the middle of a conversation. (...) '''Being on first-name terms''' does not signal that people have become closer in any way,that they find the other person likeable,or that they'll negotiate any less toughly. Especially between Germans and Dutch there often arise misunderstandings in this respect. If,for example,a manager allows himself '''to be addressed using the informal you,''' Germans tend to interpret this as a sign of a particularly good work environment,whereas the informal you is simply a conventional way of addressing people.}#to be on first-name terms|Coordinate terms}erzen}ihrzen}siezen|Derived terms}Duzbruder}Duzen}Duzfreund}Duzfreundin}duzfreundlich}Duzfreundschaft}duzfreundschaftlich}Duzkultur}Duzschwester|See also}de-decl-personal pronouns

*E*de{}|Pronunciation}IPA:/ʔeː/}De-E.OGG}Rhymes:eː}Ä|Letter}E:}#Latn-def:5|See also}list:Latin script letters/de
*-e*de{}|Pronunciation}IPA:ɛ|Etymology 1}From Middle High German -e,from Old High German -ī,from Proto-Germanic ⋆-į̄.|Suffix}-e:}#now chiefly used to form nouns from adjectives,sometimes with umlaut of the root vowel; the nouns express the quality of the adjective}•stark|Etymology 2}From Middle High German -e,a merger of various from Old High German - vocalic endings.}Further information on ''-e'' as noun plural suffix}The plural suffix  derives from a merger of from Old High German -a and from Old High German -i. Neuters usually remained unchanged in the nominative and accusative plural. The spread of the suffix to the neuter occurred by analogy with the masculine,whose declension was otherwise identical. Moreover,there were neuters ending in from Middle High German -e already in the singular; this from Middle High German -e tended to be apocopated,leading to reinterpretation of the fuller form as the plural (e.g. from Middle High German stücke > modern Stück,pl. Stücke). Another mainly neuter plural suffix is -er,which see.}Umlaut originally occurred only when the from Old High German - ending had been from Old High German -i,but from the High Middle Ages up to the present there has been a steady trend towards analogical expansion of umlaut in masculines,to the degree that umlautable monosyllables with umlautless plural have become rare (e.g. Hunde,Tage). In feminines,umlaut was seldom expanded,but the umlautless forms have switched to the weak suffix -en; therefore the ''e''-plural in feminines is now always accompanied by umlaut (excepted are the suffixes -nis and -sal,both of which vary between feminine and neuter gender). Neuters are not umlauted (the only exception being Floß).}{{rel-bottom|Suffix}-e:}#used to form the plural of some nouns; in masculines and feminines,but not in neuters,usually triggering umlaut of the root vowel}•Baum}•Nacht}•Wort}#chiefly used to form the dative of strong masculine and neuter nouns ending in a stressed syllable}•''das Haus'' → ''dem Hause'' (usually:''dem Haus'')}#used to form various declined adjective forms,notably the nominative/accusative feminine singular}•schön → ''die schöne Frau''}#used to form the 1st person singular present indicative (and subjunctive) of a verb}•gehen (geh-+-en) → ''ich gehe'' (colloquial or poetic:''ich geh'')}#used to form the 3rd person singular present subjunctive of a verb}•gehen → ''er gehe''}#used to form the 1st and 3rd person singular past subjunctive of a verb}•ging → ''ich ginge'',''er ginge''|Etymology 3}/d/coalesces with/t/of -st,unstressed/u/weakens to/ə/. See also pronunciation notes at du.|Pronoun}-e:}#colloquial contraction of+de+du+nodot1 after 2nd person singular forms of a verb.}•hast du → haste}•wärst du → wärste}•hattest du → hatteste,hattste,hatste|Etymology 4}from German personal noun suffix}Masculine weak noun endings attached to a stem,diachronically from Proto-Germanic ⋆-ô. -in is used as a female equivalent,see there.|Alternative forms}-∅|Suffix}(mask.)}#non-gloss:derives nouns referring to a person with a trait specified by the stem,from adjective or noun stems,often from toponyms}•schwedisch or Schweden→ Schwede,Schwedin}•m+:catholicus → Katholik,Katholikin}•jung → Junge}•chinesisch → Chinese,Chinesin surface analysis}•Schwaben → Schwabe,Schwäbin}•synononym [-er],[(qwhich of the two suffixes is used is not entirely predictable) they may be interchangeable in some cases]

*e-Form*de{}|Noun}(fem.)}#linguistics e-form}#}e-Form Die starke Deklination unterscheidet nach Geschlecht und Zahl des Substantivs drei Formen:die Grundform für Utrum ''god'' (gut),die t-Form für Neutrum ''godt'' (gut) und die '''e-Form''' für den Plural ''gode'' (gut).}•Based on the gender and number of the noun,the strong declension distinguishes between three forms:the lemma for common gender ''god'' (good),the t-form for neuter gender ''godt'' (good) and the '''e-form''' for the plural ''gode'' (good).}#}e-Form Steht das Substantiv in der bestimmten Form,benutzen Sie – wie Sie an den Beispielen gesehen haben – die '''e-Form''' des Adjektivs:den god'''e''' musik ''die gute Musik'',det stor'''e''' bryllup ''die große Hochzeit'',de glad'''e''' gæster ''die frohen Gäste''.}•If the noun is in the definite form,you are to use - as you have seen from the examples - the '''e-form''' of the adjective:den god'''e''' musik ''the good music'',det stor'''e''' bryllup ''the big wedding'',de glad'''e''' gæster ''the happy guests''.}#}e-Form Bei der attributiven Verwendung mit bestimmten Nomen wird unabhängig von Geschlecht und Zahl des Nomens immer die '''e-Form''' verwendet.}•In the case of attributive usage with definite nouns,the '''e-form''' is always used regardless of the gender and number of the noun.

*eh*de{}|Etymology}From Middle High German earlier,ere,originally ēr. Modern Standard German uses the lengthened form ehe (only as a conjunction).|Pronunciation}IPA:/ʔeː/}Ⓓ7/7d/De-eh.ogg}Rhymes:eː}Ä|Conjunction}eh:}#colloquial before}•Lass uns gehn,'''eh''' wir den Bus verpassen!}•Let's go before we miss the bus!|Derived terms}eh und je|Adverb}#colloquial anyway,in any case}•synononym [[sowieso],[ohnehin]],[ohnedies]}•Du brauchst nicht laufen. Du kriegst die Bahn '''eh''' nicht.}•No need to run. You won’t catch the tram '''anyways'''.}#}eh Nach der Einzellösung ist § 22 StGB für jeden Mittäter gesondert und individuell zu betrachten. Nur wer selbst unmittelbar ansetzt bzw. wer im Gesamtversuchsstadium seinen eigenen Tatbeitrag erbringt,kann wegen einer versuchten mittäterschaftlichen Tat bestraft werden. Bei der versuchten Mittäterschaft soll danach nicht die wechselseitige Zurechnung der Gesamtlösung gelten. *Ehrenmord*de{}|Etymology}[[[Ehre]+[Mord]]+[t1honor]]+[t2murder]|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈeːʁənˌmɔʁt/}Ⓓb/b8/De-Ehrenmord.ogg}Eh+ren+mord|Noun}(mask.,plural:[Ehrenmord(e)s])}#honour killing,honor killing}#}'''01.04.2010''',Ferda Ataman,https://www.tagesspiegel.de/gesellschaft/panorama/tuerkei-ehrenmord-an-einem-homosexuellen-die-angst-der-anderen/1781652.html "Ehrenmord" an einem Homosexuellen:Die Angst der anderen,Tagesspiegel}#}:Zum ersten Mal kommt es in der Türkei zu einem Prozess um den '''"Ehrenmord"''' an einem Schwulen. Der Kölner Lebensgefährte des Opfers sagt am Donnerstag vor Gericht aus. Der Hauptverdächtige ist der Vater des Getöteten.}#}'''05.08.2011''',Barbara Hans and Johannes Korge,https://www.spiegel.de/panorama/justiz/bka-studie-ein-drittel-aller-ehrenmord-opfer-sind-maennlich-a-778249.html Ein Drittel aller "Ehrenmord"-Opfer sind männlich,DER SPIEGEL}#}:Wird im Namen der "Ehre" gemordet,müssen fast immer Frauen sterben - soweit das Klischee. Doch eine BKA-Studie zeigt:Viele der Opfer in Deutschland sind Männer. Sie werden getötet,weil sie schwul sind,Ehebrecher - oder selbst einen '''"Ehrenmord"''' verweigern. |Usage notes}Sometimes written in quotation marks to indicate condemnation by implicitly expressing disbelief in the ''honour'' of the act.

*ehrpusselig*de{}|Etymology}[Ehre]+[pusselig]|Pronunciation}IPA:ˈeːɐ̯ˌpʊsəlɪç qualifier:standard}IPA:ˈeːɐ̯ˌpʊsəlɪk qualifier:common form in southern Germany,Austria,and Switzerland}ehr+pus+se+lig}Ⓓ7/7a/De-ehrpusselig.ogg|Adjective}#touchy about one's reputation}#}ehrpusselig Das verstohlene Als-ob dieses Szenenwechsels war ja auch reichlich verdächtig. Ein paar Menschen waren getötet,eine Handvoll anderer aus dem Lande gejagt; ein paar Gehöfte verbrannt,ein paar Stehbierbuden geplündert und ein paar Städte durch Bomben zerstört worden; darunter leider die wunderschöne alte Residenz der Ostindien-Kompanie Middleburg auf Walcheren. Aber man erklärte gleich,das sei nicht weiter schlimm,das zerbombte Innenviertel von Rotterdam sei längst abbruchreif gewesen,und man würde alles so schnell wieder aufbauen wie die gesprengten Brücken. Es war wie in einer Gesellschaft,wo ein Gast versehentlich ein kostbares Geschirr zerbrochen hat und die Hausfrau versichert,das bedeute nichts,es nicht das einzige,das sie besitze,außerdem sei es schon angestoßen gewesen und sollte sowieso ergänzt werden. Ein merkwürdiger '''ehrpusseliger''' Optimismus erfüllte die Leute,sich und ihrer Reputation ja nichts zu vergeben. Man begann die Straßen bereits hinten zu kehren,wenn vorn noch gekämpft wurde.

Equivalent to eigen+tum+t1own+t2-dom,compare from Dutch eigendom.|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈaɪɡəntuːm/}Ⓓa/a1/De-Eigentum.ogg}Ⓓa/a4/De-Eigentum2.ogg}Ei+gen+tum|Noun}(neut.,genitive:Eigentumes,plural:[Eigentümere])}#uncountable ownership}•Herrschaftsrecht}#countable an item of owned property,e.g. estate,belonging,etc.|Usage notes}Common translations of the word's second sense is ‘property’; however,the technical usage is narrower and does not allow for it to be used with the same objects as these terms are in English.}Outside of legal usage other areas (e.g. business administration) may use the term  for things that German law does not regard as ownership. So terms like geistiges Eigentum, not referring to corporeal objects,are strictly translationese and a misnomer and do not occur in the internal legal systems of the German-speaking countries,except as a comparative law and international law catchword. While an economic work might refer to a Markeneigentümer,legal works would refer to a Markeninhaber,as Inhaberschaft denotes any legal position as English m:ownership does.}In either cases however,the corresponding verbs eignen and innehaben are not in common use anymore but stilted; the former,for the technical sense of owning a corporeal object,is suppleted by gehören.|Derived terms}geistiges Eigentum,Eigentümer

Ist das Verfügenkönnen teils bei dem,teils bei jenem,so ist die Rechtssubjektheit gespalten. Eine Spaltung,die der Vermögenseinheit nichts abbricht. Selbst der Singularbevollmächtigte eines Handlungsfähigen ist Mitrechtssubjekt des Vermögens,auf das er kraft Vollmacht einwirken kann.:translationSince Zitelmann and Hölder,we have known that legal personality '''is a characteristic of''' the agent of a property,of the disposer of it,of him who has effective will,that legal personality rests not in the ward but in the guardian. But when legal control over a property rests partly in the former,partly in the latter,then this legal personality is divided,though this division does not affect the unitary nature of the property. The singular authorized representative of a person with the capacity to act is himself co-legal subject of the property,and he can control it by virtue of power of attorney.}#}eignen :de:authorThéophile Gautier:titleMademoiselle de Maupin:origyear1835:year1965:newversiontranslated by w:langde:Hans-Henning von Voigt:Alastair and first published by  Henry Goverts Verlag,Stuttgart 1965,then by Droemersche Verlagsanstalt Th. *einander*de{}|Etymology}From Middle High German einander,from Old High German - compound of ander|nocat1. Semantically limited by the ein to singular contexts,similar to from English one another or from English each other.}The combined form  does not inflect in modern German,and may be used unchanged in dative and accusative grammatical cases. Older forms could show inflection on the second ''ander'' portion,or on both the ''ein'' and ''ander'' portions. Any prepositions,which grammatically and semantically would apply to the second ''ander'' portion of the word,were already appearing in front of the compound term in from Old High German -,and in New High German (i.e.,modern German),prepositions are compounded onto the front of the term.|Pronunciation}IPA:aastandard}IPA:aauncommon and stiff,though etymologically correct}IPA:aacolloquial}Ⓓ9/91/De-einander.ogg|Pronoun}einander:}#each other}•Sie unterstützten '''einander''',so gut sie konnten.}•They supported '''each other''' as much as they could.|Usage notes}Prepositions are prefixed to the pronoun,thus “with each other” becomes '''''mit'''einander''. The spelling ''mit einander'' is not unfrequently seen,but is nonstandard nowadays.}As opposed to English grammar,German ''einander'' is only obligatory after prepositions,or when the reciprocity of the action is not evident from the context:

*Einlautung*de{}|Etymology}From ein+t1in+Laut+t2sound+-ung+t3-ing.|Noun}(fem.)}#linguistics the process by which a word that was borrowed from one language or dialect into a closely related other language/dialect,is adapted to the phonetic system of the latter based not on similarity of sound,but on typical etymological sound correspondences between both varieties|Usage notes}For example,the standard German word echt was first borrowed into the Ripuarian dialect as m:ech. Here the loss of ''-t'' is not a case of  because Ripuarian simply does not allow final ''-t'' after another obstruent. However,the word was then further adapted by way of  in the variant m:ääch,where the lengthening of the vowel follows such pairs as German schlecht,recht vis-à-vis Ripuarian m:schlääch,m:rääch,etc.
